A 35-year-old woman with massive painful rigidity and superim -
posed spasms in the extremities was admitted to our hospital (Osaka 
Medical College, Osaka, Japan). Her right axillary lymph nodes were 
as swollen as a tip of a thumb. The biopsy assay from a right axillary 
lymph node showed a ductal metastatic carcinoma. Furthermore, 
immunohistochemistry clearly showed the expression of estrogen 
receptor and progesterone receptor in the cancer cells (Figure 1). 
Curiously, no origin was detected in her breast by imaging analysis, in-
cluding mammography, ultrasonography, computed tomography and 
positron emission tomography–computed tomography. Therefore, 
we considered that she suffered from occult breast cancer.
Interestingly, further assessment of immunohistochemis -
try showed the massive expression of amphiphysin in the cancer 
(Figure 1). Furthermore, only anti-amphiphysin autoantibodies were 
present at a high titer in the patient’s serum on the Mayo Clinic para -
neoplastic autoantibodies test, and Hu, Ri, ANNA-3, Ma2, PCA-1, 
PCA-2, PCA-Tr, CRMP-5, amphiphysin, PQ/- and N-type VGCC, 
VGKC, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and GAD65 screening.
1 
Furthermore, electromyography showed continuous co-contraction 
of flexors and extensors in the extremities. Therefore, we diagnosed 
the patient as anti-amphiphysin autoantibodies-positive paraneoplas-
tic stiff-person syndrome (PSP) associated with occult breast cancer.
The patient did not respond to either high-dose intravenous immu-
noglobulins or simple plasma exchange therapy, but did respond rap -
idly to intravenous high-dose methyl-prednisolone (1 g/day × 3 days) 
therapy, similar to a previous report.
2 T h e r e f o r e ,  w e  f o l l o w e d  w i t h  
oral prednisolone treatment, starting at 50 mg/bodyweight (1 mg/
kg-bodyweight), and tapered it slowly. The rigidity and spasms 
promptly went into remission. After that, the patient was transferred 
to another hospital to receive radiation therapy for the cancer.

As far as we know, this is the first case where amphiphysin 
expression was detected in a metastatic lesion, which was obtained 
from occult breast cancer with PSP. The present case showed that 
high expression of amphiphysin in the metastatic lesion still caused 
the development of PSP, though the origin of the brest cancer had 
already disappeared, and steroid therapy was very effective for the 
management of the stiffness. These results showed that the autoan -
tigen in the metastatic lesion was targeted by the immune system. 
Therefore, we believe that the evaluation of autoantigen expression in 
a metastatic lesion might help with the diagnosis and treatment when 
clinicians are faced with paraneoplastic syndromes with occult cancer, 
because cancer of unknown origin is not rare in the case of paraneo -
plastic syndromes.
